mcqs.question: Why does the concurrent-connections formula use arrival rate and session duration instead of a per-request rate?
options: Because request-per-second math is always more numerically precise than any other estimation technique
Because persistent-connection systems process each request in under a millisecond, making QPS meaningless
Because it measures how many sessions are simultaneously open at any instant, which is what consumes memory and socket handles for a connection-holding system
Because session duration is generally easier to measure in production than request rate
mcqs.explanation: Concurrent connections track simultaneous open state, which is the real resource cost for a connection-holding system, unlike a per-request rate that only measures throughput. Precision and measurement-ease aren't the reasons, and processing time per request isn't the relevant factor here.

mcqs.question: 10M DAU, with 30% active during a 4-hour peak window and an average 15-minute session, gives roughly what concurrent-connection estimate?
options: About 187,500
About 3,000,000, treating the active-user count itself as the concurrent figure
About 208, treating the arrival rate alone as the final answer
About 900,000, from using session duration in minutes instead of converting to seconds
mcqs.explanation: 3,000,000 sessions over 14,400 seconds gives an arrival rate of ~208/sec; multiplied by the 900-second session duration, that's ~187,500 concurrent connections. The other options stop at an intermediate value or skip a needed unit conversion.

mcqs.question: 190,000 concurrent connections against a 20,000-connection-per-node ceiling requires how many gateway nodes, before any failover margin?
options: 9 nodes, rounding down since 9.5 rounds closer to 9
20 nodes, doubling the divided figure as a standard safety factor
95 nodes, from dividing by 2,000 instead of the stated 20,000
10 nodes
mcqs.explanation: 190,000 / 20,000 = 9.5, and capacity figures always round up, giving 10 nodes. Rounding down would undersize the fleet, and the other options use the wrong divisor or an arbitrary doubling.

mcqs.question: Why might a live trading feed favor more, smaller connection-serving nodes over fewer, larger ones, even at a higher total cost?
options: Smaller nodes are always cheaper per connection than larger ones on any real cloud provider
A dropped connection is costly for that workload, so limiting how many connections a single node failure affects matters more than raw efficiency
Larger nodes are architecturally unable to run a persistent-connection protocol like WebSocket
Regulatory requirements mandate a specific minimum node count for any financial system
mcqs.explanation: The trade is blast radius versus efficiency — a workload where a dropped connection is expensive should limit how much one node failure costs. There's no inherent cost or protocol limitation tied to node size, and no such blanket regulation.

mcqs.question: A chat system is sized using messages-per-second QPS math instead of concurrent-connection math. What breaks first?
options: The database backing the chat system, since message QPS always exceeds its write capacity first
Nothing breaks — QPS and concurrent connections scale identically for any workload
The system runs out of connection-handling capacity (memory, socket handles) long before it runs out of message-processing capacity
The load balancer, since it cannot route traffic for persistent-connection protocols at all
mcqs.explanation: Open, idle connections still consume memory and socket handles regardless of message rate, so a system sized only for message QPS runs out of connection capacity first. The database isn't guaranteed to be the bottleneck, the two metrics don't scale the same way, and load balancers do handle persistent connections.
